summary: A 1979 description of the universal host table in use at MIT and Stanford, which was meant to be better than the NIC and Tenex host tables. It also describes a compiled binary file for fast lookups.

plainLanguage.summary: Before DNS, computers kept a list of names and addresses in a file. This is a better design for such a list.

questions: why use a binary host table
subtitle: A better way to store host names, addresses, and network information.

tldr.problem: The NIC host table format was inaccurate, lacked nicknames and essential information, and was inefficient for programs to use.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 752 describes a text-based host table with separate NET and HOST entries, plus a compiled binary file format for efficient lookups on PDP-10 systems.
tldr.outcome: MIT and Stanford adopted this improved host table, which better served their needs before DNS became the standard directory service.

today: RFC 752 is not a standard and is now of historical interest. The Domain Name System (DNS) eventually replaced host tables with a more scalable, distributed directory service.

sections.title: The Problem With the Old Host Table
sections.content:
By 1979, the ARPANET needed a better directory of host computers. The official NIC host table often missed important details: it was inaccurate, omitted informal nicknames, lacked operating system and machine type information, and was awkward for software to parse.

MIT and Stanford designed their own host table to fix these problems. This RFC documents that design for others to adopt.
sections.plainLanguage: The old phone book had wrong numbers and was hard for computers to read, so MIT made a better one.

sections.title: The Text Format
sections.content:
The host table is a text file with comments and two kinds of entries. Network entries specify a network name and its numeric identifier assigned by Jon Postel. Host entries name a host, list its addresses on one or more networks, declare whether it is a user or server host, specify the operating system and machine type, and include nicknames.

For example, a host entry looks like: HOST MIT-AI,[ARPA 2/6,CHAOS 2026],SERVER,ITS,PDP10,[AI,MITAI]. This describes a host named MIT-AI reachable on both ARPANET and Chaosnet, running ITS on a PDP-10 machine, with nicknames AI and MITAI.
sections.plainLanguage: Each entry is like a business card: the computer name, addresses, what kind of computer it is, and what it does.

sections.title: The Binary File Format
sections.content:
Because recompiling every program every time the host table changed was inefficient, MIT and Stanford also defined a compiled binary file format that all programs could read from a shared location. The binary file is organized as tables: a NETWORK table listing all networks, an ADDRESS table for each network mapping network addresses to sites, a SITE table with host information, and a NAMES table for name lookups.

This binary format was specific to 36-bit PDP-10 systems and uses the SIXBIT character encoding for storage efficiency, but the text format is general purpose.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of every program reading the text file, all programs read one fast, pre-compiled file that lets them find addresses instantly.
